title: Buy and sell at the same time

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
Selling your current property and buying a new one at the same time is a balancing act: financial, logistical and timing issues intertwine. Well planned, it’s done peacefully.

This guide covers scenarios (sell first, buy first), tools to close the gap, and date coordination.

Each chapter ends with a lined “My Notes” page.

Selling your property and buying another at the same time is a balancing act: finances, logistics and timing are intertwined. This guide covers choosing the sequence, tools to bridge the gap, coordinating dates, and how to avoid double detention.

Well planned, the exercise becomes a simple series of mastered steps.

chapters.title: Sell ​​first or buy first?
chapters.objective: Choose the sequence appropriate to your risk.
chapters.html:
Choose the sequence adapted to your risk.

Everything depends on the order of operations, and each has its downside:

  • Sell first : you know your exact budget and sell without pressure, but risk having to relocate temporarily.
  • Buy first : you secure your next home, but risk paying for two properties if the old one is slow to sell.

The condition of sale (offer conditional on the sale of your property) is a tool to reduce this risk.

Everything depends on the order: sell first (exact budget known, without pressure, but risk of rehousing) or buy first (next house secured, but risk of paying for two properties). The condition of sale (offering conditionally on the sale of your property) reduces this risk.

Emilie's advice

If your budget can't accommodate two mortgages, lean toward "sell first" or use a condition of sale. Comfort of mind is often worth more than the perfect house found too soon.

chapters.title: Closing the financial gap
chapters.objective: Manage the time lag between the two transactions.
chapters.html:
Manage the gap between the two transactions.

If the dates do not coincide, or if you buy before cashing your sale, tools exist:

  • Bridge loan : temporary financing until the sale is received.
  • Line of credit : to cover a short shift.
  • Negotiation of possession dates compatible.

The bridging loan is the most common tool: it precisely covers the gap between the purchase and the sale.

If the dates do not coincide, tools fill the gap: the bridge loan (temporary financing until the sale is cleared), a line of credit, or negotiated possession dates. Talk to your mortgage broker about the bridge loan BEFORE you make an offer.

Emilie's advice

Talk to your mortgage broker about the bridge loan BEFORE making an offer. Knowing that the financial bridge is possible (and at what cost) completely changes your room for maneuver.

chapters.title: Coordinate dates and logistics
chapters.objective: Orchestrate the two closings and the move.
chapters.html:
Orchestrate the two closings and the move.

The ideal is to align the possession dates (sale and purchase) for a smooth move.

Failing that, plan:

  • Fromstorage temporary.
  • A accommodation transition.
  • A margin in the calendar.

A broker that manages both transactions can synchronize deadlines and anticipate friction points.

The ideal is to align the possession dates for a smooth move; failing that, plan for storage, transitional accommodation and a margin in the schedule. A broker that manages both transactions can synchronize deadlines and anticipate friction.

Emilie's advice

Ideally entrust the purchase AND the sale to the same broker. It sees both calendars at the same time and can set the dates to avoid a double move.

chapters.title: Avoid costly double detention
chapters.objective: Limit the risk of paying for two properties.
chapters.html:
Limit the risk of paying for two properties.

The worst scenario is to end up with two properties on the arms. Some safeguards:

  • Good price your current property so that it sells quickly.
  • Use a condition of sale for purchase when possible.
  • Negotiate flexible dates on the seller's side.
  • Keep a financial cushion to absorb a few weeks of overlap.

Anticipating the worst scenario is precisely what prevents you from experiencing it.

The worst scenario is two properties on your hands. Guardrails: Price your current property well so it sells quickly, use a condition of sale, negotiate flexible dates and keep a cushion. Don’t overestimate “just in case”: that’s what causes sales to drag on.

Emilie's advice

A well-priced and well-presented property sells faster - and it's your best protection against double ownership. Don’t overestimate “just in case”: that’s what causes sales to drag on.

chapters.title: The game plan, step by step
chapters.html:
Complete the two transactions calmly.

A successful sequence follows a clear framework:

  1. Determine the sequence (sell or buy first) depending on your risk.
  2. Validate financing and explore the bridging loan.
  3. Marketing or shop in parallel, depending on the sequence.
  4. Coordinate dates of possession.
  5. Synchronize the two closings at the notary.

Well planned, the balancing act becomes a simple series of mastered steps.

A successful sequence follows a framework: determine the sequence according to my risk, validate the financing and the bridge loan, market or shop in parallel, coordinate the dates, then synchronize the two closings. Write your plan on a page with key dates.

Emilie's advice

Write your game plan on a single page with key dates. With the big picture in hand, decisions become obvious and stress goes down.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. Determine my sequence (sell or buy first).
  2. Evaluate my ability to absorb a gap.

Within 30 days

  1. Explore the bridge loan with my mortgage broker.
  2. Coordinate possession dates.

Then

  1. Entrust both transactions to the same broker to synchronize everything.

My game plan

  1. Determine my sequence and explore the bridge loan before offering.
  2. Coordinate possession dates and maintain a safety cushion.
